facts.statement: Eolambia lived during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cenomanian,

facts.statement: The only species of Eolambia is E. caroljonesa, named by James Kirkland in 1998.
facts.quote: It contains a single species, E. caroljonesa, named by paleontologist James Kirkland in 1998.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Eolambia was discovered by Carole and Ramal Jones in 1993.
facts.quote: The type specimen of Eolambia was discovered by Carole and Ramal Jones in 1993

facts.statement: Hundreds of bones representing nearly every skeletal element have been found in both adults and juveniles.
facts.quote: Since then, hundreds of bones have been discovered from both adults and juveniles, representing nearly every element of the skeleton.

facts.statement: All known specimens of Eolambia have been found in Emery County, Utah, within the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation.
facts.quote: All of the specimens have thus far been found in Emery County, Utah, in a layer of rock known as the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation.

facts.statement: Eolambia could measure up to 6 meters in length.
facts.quote: Measuring up to 6 m long, Eolambia is a large member of its group.

facts.statement: Eolambia lived in humid floodplain forests near lakes and ate gymnosperms, ferns, and flowering plants.
facts.quote: Eolambia would have lived in a forested environment at the edge of lakes in a humid floodplain environment, feeding on gymnosperms, ferns, and flowering plants.

facts.statement: Juvenile Eolambia were preyed upon by large crocodylomorphs in the lake waters.
facts.quote: As a juvenile, Eolambia would have been preyed upon by large crocodylomorphs residing in the lake waters.

facts.statement: Mature Eolambia, at least eight to nine years old, were preyed upon by large theropods like Siats.
facts.quote: With increasing age, however, they became impervious to the crocodylomorphs, and mature individuals (at least eight to nine years in age) were preyed on by large theropods such as the neovenatorid Siats.

facts.statement: In 1979, Galton and Jensen described a fragmentary femur (BYU 2000) from Arches National Park, Utah.
facts.quote: In 1979 Peter Galton and James A. Jensen described a fragmentary right femur, BYU 2000, belonging to a hadrosaurian dinosaur discovered in sediments belonging to the Cedar Mountain Formation in Arches National Park, Utah.

facts.statement: Hadrosauroid teeth from the San Rafael Swell were described by J. Michael Parrish in 1991.
facts.quote: Various hadrosauroid teeth had also been found in quarries of small vertebrates in the western region of the San Rafael Swell, near Castle Dale in Emery County, Utah; they were described in 1991 by J. Michael Parrish.

facts.statement: Carole and Ramal Jones discovered fragmentary bones at a site in the northwestern San Rafael Swell in 1993.
facts.quote: Subsequently, in 1993, Carole Jones and her husband Ramal Jones discovered fragmentary bones in a fossil site located in the northwestern region of the Swell.

facts.statement: The discovery site was named Carol's Site in honor of Carole Jones.
facts.quote: The site, which is formally known as CEUM Locality 42em366v, would subsequently be named Carol's Site (sic) in her honour.

facts.statement: A left femur from an adult (CEUM 8786) found at Carol's Site was not described until 2012.
facts.quote: CEUM 8786, a left femur from an adult, was discovered later in Carol's Site, and was not described until 2012.

facts.statement: The Oklahoma Museum of Natural History discovered teeth of the hadrosauroid in various quarries.
facts.quote: The OMNH also made further discoveries of the hadrosauroid's teeth in various quarries.

facts.statement: James Kirkland preliminarily described the OMNH specimens in 1994.
facts.quote: Kirkland went on to preliminarily describe the specimens in 1994 in a conference abstract at the annual meeting of the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology.

facts.statement: Kirkland formally named the genus Eolambia and its species E. caroljonesa in a 1998 paper.
facts.quote: In a 1998 paper published in the bulletin of the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science, Kirkland formally named the specimens as a new genus, Eolambia, with the type and only species being Eolambia caroljonesa.

facts.statement: The name Eolambia combines the Greek word for dawn with a suffix derived from Lambeosaurus.
facts.quote: The generic name combines the Greek prefix eos/ἠώς ("dawn", "morning", implying "early") with the suffix lambia (derived from Lambeosaurus, which is in turn named after Canadian paleontologist Lawrence Lambe).

facts.statement: The name Eolambia was suggested by paleoartist Michael Skrepnick.
facts.quote: The name Eolambia was suggested by paleoartist Michael Skrepnick

facts.statement: The specific epithet caroljonesa is considered incorrect by ICZN standards, with caroljonesae being the correct spelling.
facts.quote: However, the epithet caroljonesa, following the ICZN, is incorrect and in this case the correct spelling would be caroljonesae.

facts.statement: Eolambia is the most completely known iguanodont from the Cenomanian to Santonian stages.
facts.quote: It is now the most completely-known iguanodont from between the Cenomanian and Santonian stages.

facts.statement: At least twelve individuals, including eight juveniles, were found in a quarry south of Emery.
facts.quote: At least twelve individuals, including at least eight juveniles, were discovered in a quarry south of the town of Emery, including parts from both the skull and the rest of the body.

facts.statement: Material from the Emery quarries was described in 2012 by Kirkland, McDonald, Bird, and Dodson.
facts.quote: Material from these quarries was described in 2012 by Kirkland along with Andrew McDonald, John Bird, and Peter Dodson, who also provided an updated diagnosis for Eolambia based on this material.

facts.statement: Researchers caution that a deep dentary specimen might represent a distinct hadrosauroid rather than an unusual Eolambia.
facts.quote: Although it is possible that this individual represents an unusual Eolambia specimen, McDonald and colleagues cautioned that it may represent a distinct hadrosauroid that differs in the morphology of the dentary from Eolambia (albeit one that is not suggested by any of the other materials at the quarry).

facts.statement: The Field Museum of Natural History excavated south of Emery from 2009 to 2010.
facts.quote: The Field Museum of Natural History (FMNH) also conducted excavations south of the town of Emery from 2009 to 2010, with permits from the Utah Geological Survey.

facts.statement: A hip and vertebrae specimen (FMNH PR 3847) was described in 2017 by McDonald, Gates, Zanno, and Makovicky.
facts.quote: One of these plaster jackets, containing elements from the hip and vertebrae, was given the specimen number FMNH PR 3847; the specimen was subsequently described by McDonald along with Terry Gates, Lindsay Zanno, and Peter Makovicky in 2017.

facts.statement: Eolambia fossils are found exclusively in the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation.
facts.quote: All of the localities that Eolambia were discovered in belong to the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation.

facts.statement: In 2007, researchers dated the volcanic ash layer at the Cifelli #2 Quarry to 96.7 ± 0.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Subsequently, in 2007, James Garrison and colleagues dated the volcanic ash layer passing through the Cifelli #2 Quarry – which is likely the same layer dated previously by Cifelli and colleagues – to 96.7 ± 0.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Analysis of pollen assemblages suggests the deposits where Eolambia lived span the boundary between the Albian and Cenomanian stages.
facts.quote: Garrison and colleagues also re-analyzed the pollen assemblage from localities throughout the Mussentuchit, concluding that the assemblage spans the Albian-Cenomanian boundary.

facts.statement: Eolambia is classified as a large hadrosauroid dinosaur.
facts.quote: Eolambia is a large hadrosauroid.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated in 2016 that Eolambia reached a body length of 6 meters and a weight of 1 metric ton.
facts.quote: In 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated a body length of 6 m and a weight of 1 MT for Eolambia

facts.statement: An adult Eolambia specimen was estimated in 2008 to be 5.2 meters long with a hip height of 2 meters.
facts.quote: Earlier, in 2008, an adult specimen was estimated as having a length of 5.2 m and a height at the hip of 2 m.

facts.statement: Eolambia possessed a crestless skull with a shape similar to that of Equijubus and Probactrosaurus.
facts.quote: The crestless skull of Eolambia has a similar overall shape to those of Equijubus and Probactrosaurus.

facts.statement: The tips of Eolambia's premaxillae feature two tooth-like structures called denticles, a trait shared with Protohadros.
facts.quote: At the tip of each premaxilla, there are two tooth-like structures known as denticles, which is also seen in its closest relative Protohadros.

facts.statement: A distinguishing feature of Eolambia is the concave profile of its maxillary tooth row when viewed from the side.
facts.quote: One of the characteristics used to distinguish Eolambia is the concave profile of the tooth row of the maxilla when viewed from the side

facts.statement: Eolambia's jaws contained tightly packed teeth, with 32 sockets in the upper jaw holding three teeth each and 30 sockets in the lower jaw holding four teeth each.
facts.quote: At any given time, each of the 32 maxillary tooth sockets holds three teeth, while each of the 30 dentary tooth sockets holds four teeth.

facts.statement: In Eolambia, two of the teeth within each jaw socket were replacement teeth while the others were active teeth.
facts.quote: Out of these, two of the teeth in each socket are replacement teeth like those of Probactrosaurus; the others are active teeth.

facts.statement: The crowns of Eolambia's teeth possessed small, denticle-like serrations on their front and rear edges.
facts.quote: All of the crowns also bear small, denticle-like serrations on the front and rear edges, which is also seen in Probactrosaurus.

facts.statement: The Cifelli #2 Quarry is a specific locality associated with the river channel system where Eolambia fossils were found.
facts.quote: The Cifelli #2 Quarry is associated with this system.

facts.statement: Fossils of Eolambia from the Cifelli #2 quarry are blackened due to replacement by minerals including calcite, quartz, pyrite, and carbonate-hydroxyapatite.
facts.quote: In the Cifelli #2 quarry, the bones themselves are blackened, having been replaced by calcite, quartz, pyrite, and carbonate-hydroxyapatite.

facts.statement: Eolambia possessed highly opisthocoelous cervical vertebrae with strongly convex front ends and concave back ends, a trait shared with other styracosternans.
facts.quote: Like Equijubus, Probactrosaurus, Gongpoquansaurus, and other styracosternans, Eolambia has cervical vertebrae which are very opisthocoelous, meaning that their front ends are strongly convex while their back ends are strongly concave.

facts.statement: The third cervical vertebra of Eolambia uniquely had its front end positioned slightly higher than its back end, a feature not found in any other known cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: Unusually, the front end of the third cervical is set slightly higher than the back end, which is not seen in any other cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: The rearmost cervical vertebrae of Eolambia featured deep depressions between postzygapophyses and steeply angled neural spine margins that formed prominent spike-like projections.
facts.quote: In the rearmost cervicals, there is also a deep depression separating the postzygapophyses, and the neural spines have steeply-angled front margins, which has the effect of creating prominent spike-like projections.

facts.statement: The initial dorsal vertebrae of Eolambia resembled cervical vertebrae but possessed taller, prong-like neural spines.
facts.quote: The first few dorsal vertebrae are similar to the cervical vertebrae, but have taller and more prong-like neural spines.

facts.statement: Most dorsal vertebrae in Eolambia were amphiplatyan, characterized by being flat at both ends.
facts.quote: The rest are amphiplatyan, meaning that they are flat at both ends.

facts.statement: The best-preserved sacrum of Eolambia found so far contains seven vertebrae.
facts.quote: Among the Eolambia specimens found to date, the best-preserved sacrum includes seven vertebrae.

facts.statement: Because the specimen with seven sacral vertebrae was immature and hadrosaur sacral counts increase with age, adult Eolambia likely possessed more than seven sacrals.
facts.quote: Given that this individual is immature, and hadrosaurs increase their sacral vertebra count with age, adults may have had more sacrals.

facts.statement: Eolambia's tail vertebrae were amphicoelous, meaning both their front and back ends were concave.
facts.quote: The caudal (tail) vertebrae are amphicoelous, having both the front and back ends being concave.

facts.statement: The scapular blade of Eolambia was nearly rectangular with straight sides meeting the blade end at almost a right angle, similar to Probactrosaurus.
facts.quote: Like Probactrosaurus, the scapular blade of Eolambia is nearly rectangular, with the sides of the blade being straight and meeting the end of the blade at an almost-right angle.

facts.statement: Eolambia's humerus bowed toward the midline and featured a prominently thickened deltopectoral crest.
facts.quote: The humerus is bowed towards the midline, and the deltopectoral crest on the humerus is prominently thickened.

facts.statement: Eolambia possessed a hand with five digits.
facts.quote: The hand has five digits.

facts.statement: Eolambia's hand metacarpals showed distinct shapes: the second was curved, the third straight, and the fourth strongly curved.
facts.quote: Among the metacarpal bones of the hand, the second is curved, the third is straight, and the fourth is strongly curved.

facts.statement: The first digit claw of Eolambia was distinctively conical, a trait shared with Iguanodon, Probactrosaurus, and other basal iguanodonts.
facts.quote: Like Iguanodon, Probactrosaurus, and other basal iguanodonts, the claw on the first digit is distinctively conical.

facts.statement: Eolambia's second and third hand claws were hoof-like, with the third claw having roughened side flanges, a feature also found in other iguanodonts.
facts.quote: The second and third claws are hoof-like, with the third claw bearing roughened flanges on its sides – a trait also shared with other iguanodonts.

facts.statement: Eolambia had a hip socket that was quite large relative to the ilium compared to other iguanodonts.
facts.quote: The hip socket itself is quite large relative to the ilium for an iguanodont.

facts.statement: A distinctive flange on the top surface of Eolambia's ilium is a trait shared with an unnamed hadrosauroid from the Woodbine Formation.
facts.quote: A distinctive flange is present along the top surface of the ilium, a trait which is shared with an unnamed hadrosauroid from the Woodbine Formation.

facts.statement: The postacetabular process of Eolambia's ilium tapered at the rear without any break in its top margin.
facts.quote: The postacetabular (i.e. located behind the hip socket) process of the ilium tapers at its rear with no break in its top margin.

facts.statement: The forward-projecting process on Eolambia's pubis expanded toward the front, a trait shared with Probactrosaurus, Gongpoquansaurus, and other iguanodonts.
facts.quote: On the pubis, the forward-projecting process expands towards the front, like Probactrosaurus, Gongpoquansaurus, and other iguanodonts.

facts.statement: In adult Eolambia, the ischium shaft was characteristically straight (unlike the curved shaft in juveniles common among iguanodonts) and bore a compressed 'boot' expanded forward at the bottom.
facts.quote: The shaft of the ischium is characteristically straight in adults (juveniles have a curved shaft, which is more common among iguanodonts), and the bottom of the shaft bears a compressed "boot" that is expanded forwards.

facts.statement: Eolambia's femur bowed outward like the humerus, but characteristically had a straight bottom half.
facts.quote: Like the humerus, the femur is bowed, but outwards. However, characteristically, the bottom half of the femur is straight.

facts.statement: The fourth trochanter on Eolambia's femur was vertically tall and triangular, similar to Probactrosaurus and other iguanodonts but different from more basal ornithopods.
facts.quote: The fourth trochanter, located halfway down the femur, is vertically tall and triangular, similar to Probactrosaurus, Gongpoquansaurus, and other iguanodonts but dissimilar to more basal ornithopods.

facts.statement: Eolambia's foot possessed four digits.
facts.quote: The foot has four digits.

facts.statement: Eolambia's second, third, and fourth foot claws were uniformly broad, flat, and hoof-like, similar to the hand claws.
facts.quote: As with the second and third claws on the hand, the second, third, and fourth claws of the foot are uniformly broad, flat, and hoof-like.

facts.statement: Kirkland initially classified Eolambia as a member of the Hadrosauridae family based on a definition established in 1993.
facts.quote: In Kirkland's initial description of Eolambia, he considered it to be a member of the Hadrosauridae, as defined by David B. Weishampel, David B. Norman, and Dan Grigorescu in 1993.

facts.statement: Kirkland assigned Eolambia to the subfamily Euhadrosauria, which includes the common ancestor of Saurolophinae and Lambeosaurinae and all its descendants.
facts.quote: Kirkland further assigned Eolambia to the Euhadrosauria, defined by Weishampel and colleagues to include the common ancestor of Hadrosaurinae (now the Saurolophinae) and Lambeosaurinae

facts.statement: Kirkland debated whether Eolambia was a basal member of the Lambeosaurinae or their sister group, noting that recognizing it as a lambeosaurine would require redefining the subfamily.
facts.quote: Within the Hadrosauridae, Kirkland further considered Eolambia to either be a basal member of the Lambeosaurinae, or the sister group of Lambeosaurinae.

facts.statement: Jason Head re-evaluated the classification of Eolambia in 2001 using specimens from the OMNH collection.
facts.quote: In 2001, Jason Head re-evaluated the phylogenetic position of Eolambia based on specimens stored at the OMNH.

facts.statement: Head concluded that Eolambia is a basal member of Hadrosauroidea outside the Hadrosauridae, closely related to Probactrosaurus.
facts.quote: Thus, Head concluded that Eolambia was a basal member of the Hadrosauroidea, outside of the Hadrosauridae, a conclusion supported by a phylogenetic analysis finding it to be a non-hadrosaurid hadrosauroid closely related to Probactrosaurus.

facts.statement: Head found that Eolambia had broader, more asymmetrical teeth and that subadults possessed only two teeth per position, unlike hadrosaurids.
facts.quote: Head also demonstrated that the teeth of Eolambia were broader and more asymmetrical than Kirkland had assumed; he also noted that subadults only possessed two teeth per tooth position, unlike hadrosaurids

facts.statement: Eolambia possessed seven sacral vertebrae, whereas derived hadrosaurids have eight or more.
facts.quote: Head further showed that Eolambia possessed seven sacral vertebrae, unlike eight or more in derived hadrosaurids

facts.statement: Kirkland suggested that basal hadrosaurids like Eolambia may have developed their antitrochanter later in life compared to derived hadrosaurids.
facts.quote: Kirkland noted the possibility that basal hadrosaurids developed their antitrochanter later in life than derived hadrosaurids such as Hypacrosaurus.

facts.statement: Horner and colleagues identified Eolambia as a non-hadrosaurid hadrosauroid that was the sister group to Protohadros.
facts.quote: They found Eolambia again as a non-hadrosaurid hadrosauroid, albeit as the sister group to Protohadros.

facts.statement: Horner and colleagues noted coarse denticles on the dentary teeth and a weakly expanded coronoid process as features differentiating Eolambia from hadrosaurids.
facts.quote: They also identified additional characteristics differentiating Eolambia from hadrosaurids: there are coarse denticles on the teeth of the dentary, and the coronoid process is weakly expanded.

facts.statement: In 2012, Holtz classified Eolambia as a primitive member of the Styracosterna alongside Altirhinus.
facts.quote: In 2012, Holtz classified Eolambia as a primitive member of the Styracosterna along with Altirhinus.

facts.statement: McDonald based the sister relationship between Eolambia and Probactrosaurus on a straight quadrate with a curved top end and nearly parallel scapular blade margins.
facts.quote: This close relationship was based on two shared characteristics: the quadrate being straight save for the top end, which is curved backwards; and the top and bottom margins of the scapular blade being nearly parallel.

facts.statement: McDonald and colleagues later determined in 2017 that Jeyawati was more derived than previously thought.
facts.quote: However, McDonald and colleagues found the latter to be more derived in 2017.

facts.statement: Gates and colleagues supported the sister relationship between Choyrodon and Eolambia with a trapezoidally-shaped occiput and two shared tooth traits.
facts.quote: Three characteristics supported this sister relationship: a trapezoidally-shaped occiput, and two shared traits of the teeth.

facts.statement: Eggshells possibly belonging to Eolambia have been found at various localities alongside isolated teeth.
facts.quote: Eggshells possibly belonging to Eolambia have been discovered at various localities alongside isolated teeth.

facts.statement: The Eolambia eggshells have reticular surface patterns and a thickness of 2 mm.
facts.quote: They have reticular (net-like) surface patterns, and have a thickness of 2 mm.

facts.statement: Eolambia growth changes are well-documented because the species is known from both juvenile and adult specimens.
facts.quote: Being known from a variety of juvenile and adult specimens, the changes Eolambia underwent as it grew are well-documented.

facts.statement: The number of maxilla teeth in Eolambia increased from 23 in juveniles to 33 in adults.
facts.quote: The number of teeth in the maxilla increased with age, from 23 in a juvenile to 33 in an adult.

facts.statement: The number of dentary teeth in Eolambia increased from 18 to 22 in juveniles to 25 to 30 in adults.
facts.quote: A similar increase occurred in the dentary teeth, from 18–22 in juveniles to 25–30 in adults.

facts.statement: Adult Eolambia possess faint secondary ridges on their dentary tooth crowns, which are absent in juveniles.
facts.quote: While juveniles lack secondary ridges on the crowns of their dentary teeth, faint secondary ridges are present in adults.

facts.statement: The size of the ischial "boot" in Eolambia increased with age, according to Kirkland.
facts.quote: The size of the "boot" of the ischium also increased with age, as documented by Kirkland.

facts.statement: McDonald and colleagues reported in 2017 that a rib from specimen FMNH PR 3847 showed extensive bone remodeling.
facts.quote: Results from a histological analysis performed on a rib from specimen FMNH PR 3847 were reported by McDonald and colleagues in 2017.

facts.statement: A histological analysis of an Eolambia rib showed five visible lines of arrested growth (LAGs) on the bone interior where layered growth was visible.
facts.quote: On the outer surface of the bone, osteons have almost completely replaced the interior of the bone; the layered growth of the bone is more visible on the interior of the bone, where five lines of arrested growth (LAGs) are visible.

facts.statement: The unfused sutures between cervical and dorsal vertebrae centra and neural spines, as well as between sacral centra and ribs, are consistent with the growth stage of the Eolambia specimen.
facts.quote: This is consistent with the unfused sutures between the centra and neural spines in the cervical and dorsal vertebrae, and the unfused sutures between the sacral centra and their corresponding ribs.

facts.statement: Eolambia lived between 121.4 and 93.9 million years ago during the Aptian and Cenomanian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Cenomanian (121.4 to 93.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: Eolambia is classified within the parent group Hadrosauroidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Hadrosauroidea

facts.statement: Eolambia belongs to the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: The genus Eolambia was named by Kirkland in 1998.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Eolambia (genus), Kirkland 1998

facts.statement: Eolambia lived on a poorly-drained floodplain near a system of large, perennial lakes.
facts.quote: Sedimentological data from the Mussentuchit Member indicates that Eolambia lived on a poorly-drained floodplain, around a system of large, perennial lakes.

facts.statement: At a paleolatitude of 46° N, the environment where Eolambia lived had a mean surface temperature of 40 to 45°C, which was 6 to 8°C warmer than today.
facts.quote: With a paleolatitude of 46° N, the Mussentuchit would have had a warm mean surface temperature of 40 - 45 C, about 6 - 8 C warmer than the present day, according to general circulation models.

facts.statement: Evidence of scavenging includes severed Eolambia tibiae with tooth marks found in the Cifelli #2 quarry.
facts.quote: Before burial, scavengers could have disrupted the skeletal material, which is evident in the severed Eolambia tibiae bearing tooth marks discovered in the Cifelli #2 quarry.

facts.statement: The abundance of juvenile Eolambia fossils suggests that larger individuals were too big to be preyed upon by crocodilians.
facts.quote: The abundance of juvenile Eolambia specimens in the lakeside fossil material supports this hypothesis; larger Eolambia would have been invulnerable to crocodilians.

facts.statement: Larger Eolambia were likely vulnerable to predation by the large neovenatorid theropod Siats.
facts.quote: Larger Eolambia would have been vulnerable to the large neovenatorid theropod Siats, which was discovered by expeditions from the FMNH.

facts.statement: The nodosaurid dinosaur Animantarx was found near the type specimen of Eolambia at Carol's Site.
facts.quote: As for herbivorous dinosaurs, the nodosaurid Animantarx was discovered in Carol's Site, near the type specimen of Eolambia.

facts.statement: Researchers Kirkland, Cifelli, and colleagues proposed that Eolambia arrived in North America from Asia during the Cenomanian, replacing native fauna.
facts.quote: Kirkland, Cifelli, and colleagues noted that the fauna of the Mussentuchit – iguanodonts, pachycephalosaurs, and ceratopsians – bears strong similarities to contemporary Asian faunas. They proposed that Eolambia was part of an influx of Asian dinosaurs into North America during the Cenomanian, which supplanted the earlier low-diversity native fauna.

facts.statement: Other researchers contradict the Asian origin hypothesis by suggesting that the North American Protohadros is the closest relative of Eolambia.
facts.quote: However, the results of Horner and colleagues, Prieto-Márquez, and McDonald and colleagues, which consider the North American Protohadros to be the closest relative of Eolambia, contradict this hypothesis.
